mossy fiber synaptic reorganization is a necessary but insufficient cause of epileptic seizures.
recurrent excitation generated through the mossy fiber sprout pathway contributes to the epileptogenic process.

recurrent excitation generated in the dentate by mossy fiber axonal sprouting is not a sufficient cause of epileptogenesis, but may be a contributing factor in the emergence of seizures in a complex system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

recurrent excitation generated in the dentate by sprouting of the granule cell mossy fiber pathway is a critical factor in seizure susceptibility and epileptogenesis, but that it is an emergent property, not a fixed feature of the sprouted circuit.

recurrent excitation is a fundamental feature of complex systems, but that recurrent excitation generated in a complex circuit by mossy fiber axon sprouting is a conditional emergent property of the circuit, and thus is not a necessary consequence of mossy fiber sprout formation.

the recurrent excitation generated in the epileptic brain by mossy fiber synaptic reorganization emerges only intermittently and conditionally, and is a consequence of the emergent properties of complex systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the recurrent excitatory synaptic connections formed by mossy fibers after seizure or injury can be viewed as an emergent property that arises from the interaction between an injury or insult and the complex system properties of the hippocampal circuit.

the recurrent excitation generated in the epileptic hippocampus by mossy fiber reorganization is an emergent property that is only conditionally present and can only be detected in a fraction of cells and only intermittently.

the functional consequences of circuit reorganization emerge only intermittently, and are not a simple consequence of the anatomy of a circuit, but depend on the dynamics and the properties of the network in which the circuit is embedded.
